name: inglés nicaragüense / Nicaraguan English
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: O'Neil, Wayne. 1991. El inglés nicaragüense II. Wani: Revista del Caribe Nicaragüense 10: 18-37. Managua: CIDCA-UCA.
catalog_locator: Sec. 5.3 'Acento prosódico', p. 25 right column (image-only), continuing p. 26 left column
catalog_quote: 5.3. Acento prosódico Desde el punto de vista de su acentuación prosódica, el inglés nicaragüense es muy parecido al inglés internacional, excepto en un aspecto muy claro: la acentuación prosódica de los nombres compuestos. Como fue señalado originalmente en McLean y Past (1976), los compuestos simples en el inglés nicaragüense tiene el principal acento prosódico en la segunda parte – en la cabeza, en lugar de en la primera parte como en inglés internacional, e. g.: [3] a. head-áche b. type-wríter c. baby-síster d. one-mínded (i. e., 'single-minded') e. test-glásses (i. e., 'prescripcion glasses') f. fisher-mán El acento prosódico del inglés nicaragüense no ha sido hasta ahora investigado adicionalmente; sería, por consiguiente, interesante estudiar más profundamente las características de este aspecto de su fonología. Por ejemplo, hay consecuencias adicionales, como uno podría esperarse, de este rasgo de la acentuación de las palabras compuestas en casos de composición más intrincada. ¿Cómo se ajustan los acentos de las palabras (incluyendo las compuestas) los unos a los otros, al nivel de la estructura de la frase?

new_statements.translation: 5.3. Stress. From the point of view of its stress (prosodic accentuation), Nicaraguan English is very similar to international English, except in one very clear respect: the stressing of compound nouns. As originally pointed out in McLean and Past (1976), simple compounds in Nicaraguan English have the main stress on the second part - on the head - instead of on the first part as in international English, e.g. head-áche, type-wríter, baby-síster, one-mínded, test-glásses, fisher-mán. The stress of Nicaraguan English has not so far been investigated further

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress placement is essentially that of (metropolitan) English, i.e. lexically determined English stress; the one systematic difference noted is that compounds carry primary stress on their second (head) element rather than the first (fisher-mán, head-áche). McLean & Past 1976 (p. 92) phrase the same observation more broadly: 'stress frequently is shifted to the final syllable' (water /wat'á/, businessman /biznizmán/).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds right-prominent (main stress on the head/second member) unlike other Englishes; McLean & Past's list also shows shoemaker /šuméka/ with stress on the second member's first syllable rather than the word-final syllable. O'Neil notes stress interaction in more complex compounds and at phrase level is uninvestigated; intonation said to differ markedly from European English but undescribed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical and compound stress); author explicitly leaves phrase-level accent and intonation open. Supported first-hand by O'Neil & Honda 1987 (Wani 6: 50, 'compound words generally have the heavier stress accent.. on their second part') and McLean & Past 1976 (LACUS Forum 3: 92, 'stress frequently is shifted to the final syllable'), both also. APiCS (Bartens 2013) records 'No tone distinctions' and is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All three first-hand sources describe the creole English of Bluefields and the southern Atlantic (Miskito) Coast of Nicaragua, called 'Nicaraguan English' (O'Neil; O'Neil & Honda), 'Bluefields English/creole' (McLean & Past, McLean a native speaker from Bluefields) and 'Nicaraguan Creole English' / 'Miskito Coast Creole' (Bartens, Holm) = Glottolog nica1252, ISO bzk. The divergent Rama Cay variety (Assadi 1983, Young-Davy 1992) is not the basis of any statement quoted here.

sources.note: Sec. 5 'La fonología del inglés nicaragüense', 5.3 'Acento prosódico' (p. 25-26): prosodic accentuation is very similar to international English except that simple compounds carry main stress on the second element (the head): head-áche, type-wríter, baby-síster, one-mínded, test-glásses, fisher-mán (citing McLean & Past 1976); adds that Nicaraguan English stress has not been further investigated and raises phrase-level questions.

sources.citation: O'Neil, Wayne & Maya Honda. 1987. Nicaraguan English / El inglés nicaragüense. Wani 6: 49-60 (Managua: CIDCA).
sources.note: p. 50 'Stress accent': 'There are many interesting metrical characteristics of Nicaraguan English, but one of the most obvious is that compound words generally have the heavier stress accent, or louder pronunciation on their second part rather than on the first (as in other varieties of English). For example, fisherman is pronounced /fishamán/, not /físhaman/'. Spanish version p. 57.

sources.citation: McLean, Guillermo & Ray Past. 1977 [1976]. Some characteristics of Bluefields English. In Robert J. Di Pietro & Edward L. Blansitt Jr. (eds.), The Third LACUS Forum 1976, 87-94. Columbia, SC: Hornbeam Press.
sources.note: p. 92 (p. 104), end of 'Some features of the phonology': 'Lastly, stress frequently is shifted to the final syllable.' Examples with final stress marks: water /wat'á/, drayman /drēmán/, fisherman /fišamán/, businessman /biznizmán/, bossman /basmán/ (but shoemaker /šuméka/).
